summary: A CCC-built stone lookout atop a peak once called Lookout Mountain, renamed for President Coolidge in 1934, still staffed and reachable by a narrow drive-up gravel road.

facts.design: Three-story stone lookout, built by the Civilian Conservation Corps

staffing.status: still staffed, used as a fire lookout and dispatch point

access.note: Drive-up via a 1.7-mile narrow, blind-curved gravel spur off SD Highway 87; open to visitors during summer daylight hours, typically 9am-5pm.

visit.trail_note: Gravel spur road off SD 87, about 3 miles south of US 16A; narrow with sharp drop-offs, not suited to large vehicles.

facts.agency: South Dakota Game, Fish, and Parks

events.note: Newspaper reference to an existing fire station on the peak (then called Sheep Mountain).
60-foot log tower built on the peak (then called Lookout Mountain), replacing an earlier steel tower, per contemporary newspaper accounts.
Peak officially renamed Mount Coolidge by the U.S. Geographic Board, after President Coolidge.

National Historic Lookout Register dates the current stone lookout to 1939; a 1939 newspaper article still described the tower as the 1928 log structure, so the stone tower's exact completion date is unclear.
Forest Fire Lookout Association dates the current three-story stone lookout, built by the CCC, to 1940-41.
Added to the National Historic Lookout Register, June 9, 2017.

evidence.supports: Early fire station on the peak (as Sheep Mountain), bear encounter, 1928 log tower, renaming to Mount Coolidge in 1934, 1939 description of log tower
evidence.quote: Jack was stationed there long before President Coolidge came here, the place being known as Lookout Mountain and Sheep Mountain.

evidence.supports: Official renaming by U.S. Geographic Board, Feb 1934
evidence.quote: The United States today officially recognized 'Mount Coolidge.' The peak, in Custer county, South Dakota, sometimes called Lookout mountain or Sheep mountain, had been noted by its new name by the United States geographic board.

evidence.supports: 1939 account still describing a log tower built in 1928
evidence.quote: The tower is of log construction, being built in 1928 to replace an old steel tower.

evidence.supports: Stone lookout built by CCC in 1939, still staffed for fire spotting and dispatch, 6,023 ft
evidence.quote: Perched at 6,023 feet, Mount Coolidge Fire Tower is the park's classic high perch: a stone lookout built by the Civilian Conservation Corps in 1939 that's still staffed for fire spotting and dispatch.

evidence.supports: 1922 wooden tower, present three-story stone structure built 1940-41 by CCC, staffed, list of known lookout personnel
evidence.quote: 1922: 50' wooden tower. The present 3-story stone lookout structure was built in 1940-1941 by the Civilian Conservation Corps. It is staffed. Known lookout personnel: 1920s: John Sheehan; 1933: Frank Walsh; 1939-1941: Clarence Mann; 1941-1954: Lamont McKinney; 1958-1961: Gayle Dryden; 1963: Gayle Duncan; 1966: Fred Herbert; 1983-1990: Jerry & Lynn Loomer.
This unique stone lookout was built in 1939 by CCC workers.

evidence.supports: One of the last CCC projects in the late 1930s, local stone, still used as fire lookout/dispatch, 6,023 ft
evidence.quote: The Mount Coolidge Lookout and Fire Tower was one of the last projects completed by the Civilian Conservation Corps in the late 1930s. Built of local stone, the tower rests atop a 6,023-foot peak on the way to Blue Bell Lodge and is still used today as a fire lookout and dispatch center.

evidence.supports: Drive-up gravel road access, narrow with blind curves, daylight summer hours
evidence.quote: As I stated about, you will find yourself on a 1.7 mile very narrow and blind curve gravel road... It is only open during the daylight hours (typically 9am-5pm) during the summer.

resolved_conflicts.explanation: NHLR and Parkwolf give 1939 for the current stone lookout; the Forest Fire Lookout Association gives 1940-41. A July 1939 newspaper article describes the tower on the mountain as still being the 1928 log structure, which suggests the stone tower may not have been complete until after 1939, closer to the FFLA's 1940-41 dating. The story presents both figures rather than picking one.

notes_for_editor: Build year of the current stone tower is disputed between 1939 (NHLR, Parkwolf) and 1940-41 (FFLA); a 1939 newspaper excerpt describing a log tower adds ambiguity. Height given in the brief (15.2 m) likely refers to the tower structure; elevation sources consistently give the peak as 6,023 ft, slightly different from the brief's 6,003 ft NHLR figure -- flagged as a minor discrepancy, not corrected since NHLR is the brief's own source.
